To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the genetic variants with large effects on the phenotypes are highly penetrant and are readily identified in the affected individuals and their families, and that the variants with modest effects are less penetrant and are often found as common genetic variants in the general population.

(1) the genetic variants exerting the largest effect sizes on a phenotype are highly penetrant and are best analyzed through cosegregational analyses; (2) the genetic variants with small effect sizes are less penetrant and are more difficult to ascertain through cosegregation analysis; and (3) the genetic variants that exert small effect sizes are expected to show the largest influence from the genetic backgrounds and the environment.

1) the effect sizes of genetic variants follow a gradient from small to large and 2) the causal role of genetic variants with small effect sizes can be inferred through the use of a statistical approach called Mendelian randomization, which is an extension of the Mendelian randomization.3,4
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic architecture of human traits.
the identification of genetic variants that are causally associated with the development of complex diseases.
the genetic architecture of complex diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic variants in question are causative for the disease in question in the context of the specific genetic backgrounds and environment in the study populations.
the genetic variant is causally associated with the disease phenotype in the context of a specific genetic background and a specific environmental condition.
the causal relationship between a variant and the phenotype is probabilistic and conditional on the genetic and environmental backgrounds in which the variants and the phenotype are expressed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a new method to estimate the genetic effects of variants with small to moderate effects.
we found a strong association of the rs10757278 variant with the risk of developing T2D.
we are trying to establish the causality of genetic variants in a more rigorous manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic variants exert a gradient of effect sizes, ranging from small to large, which is reflected in the degree of causality.
the genetic backgrounds and the environmental factors are likely to influence the effect sizes of a genetic variant, which is particularly relevant when the effect sizes are modest.
a genetic variant can exert a large effect on a trait, even if it is not a Mendelian variant and even in the presence of genetic and environmental modifiers.
